title: Sickle cell disease: vaso-occlusive crisis (adult)
subject: haematology-oncology
summary: Assess and give analgesia within 60 minutes of arrival, tailor opioids to the patient's previous needs and reassess every 30 to 60 minutes, give oxygen only if hypoxic, avoid overhydration, watch closely for acute chest syndrome, and start or optimise hydroxyurea.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Acute pain in the back, chest, limbs or abdomen in a person with sickle cell disease (HbSS, HbS-beta thalassaemia, HbSC). Triggers: infection, dehydration, cold, exertion, alcohol, pregnancy.
No test confirms or excludes a painful crisis: believe the patient's report of pain and severity.

Red flags needing urgent evaluation: fever 38.5 C or more, chest pain, breathlessness or hypoxia (acute chest syndrome), new neurological deficit (stroke), priapism, sudden fall in Hb (splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis), RUQ pain with jaundice, severe headache.
In India, SCD is most common in tribal populations of central, western and southern states; the Arab-Indian haplotype often has higher HbF, but crises and acute chest syndrome still occur.

sections.title: First hour
items: Triage as urgent. Assess pain and give the first analgesic dose within 60 minutes of arrival (ASH 2020); use SC or intranasal routes if IV access is delayed.

Severe pain: parenteral opioid, using the individual care plan or previously effective dose where known; otherwise morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV or SC. Reassess every 30 to 60 minutes and redose until pain is controlled.
Add paracetamol and, if renal function and bleeding risk allow, a short NSAID course of 5 to 7 days (ASH 2020).
Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 95% on air or below the patient's baseline; routine oxygen gives no benefit.
Fluids: encourage oral intake. Use IV fluid only for dehydration or inability to drink, at no more than maintenance rate; avoid repeated boluses (risk of pulmonary oedema and acute chest syndrome).

sections.title: Investigations
items: FBC and reticulocyte count compared with steady-state values (low reticulocytes suggest aplastic crisis, often parvovirus B19), renal and liver function, LDH.
Group and screen with extended red cell phenotype if transfusion is possible (alloimmunisation is common).
If febrile or chest symptoms: blood cultures, chest X-ray, urine culture, and a malaria test in endemic areas.
Continuous or frequent SpO2 monitoring; blood gas if SpO2 is falling.

sections.title: Ongoing inpatient care
items: Give opioids regularly or by patient-controlled analgesia rather than only as needed; prescribe laxatives and antiemetics, monitor sedation and respiratory rate, and keep naloxone available.
Refractory pain despite opioids: subanaesthetic ketamine infusion 0.1 to 0.3 mg/kg/hour (maximum 1 mg/kg/hour) in a monitored setting, or regional anaesthesia for localised pain (ASH 2020).
Do not use corticosteroids for pain (rebound pain and complications). Avoid pethidine (seizure risk).
Incentive spirometry every 2 hours while awake to prevent acute chest syndrome; early mobilisation.
Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) for hospitalised adults unless contraindicated; folic acid 5 mg daily.
Look for and treat precipitants, especially infection and malaria.

sections.title: Acute chest syndrome and transfusion
items: Acute chest syndrome: new pulmonary infiltrate with fever, chest pain, cough, tachypnoea or hypoxia; often develops 24 to 72 hours into a painful crisis. It is an emergency needing HDU or ICU care.
Treat with IV ceftriaxone plus an oral macrolide (azithromycin), oxygen to keep SpO2 at 95% or more, incentive spirometry, analgesia and careful fluid balance.
Simple red cell transfusion if Hb has fallen by more than 1 g/dL below baseline; do not raise Hb above 10 g/dL (hyperviscosity).

Urgent exchange transfusion for rapid progression: SpO2 below 90% despite oxygen, increasing respiratory distress, spreading infiltrates, or falling Hb despite simple transfusion; also for acute stroke.
Uncomplicated painful crises do not need transfusion. Other indications: symptomatic severe anaemia, splenic sequestration or aplastic crisis.

sections.title: Escalate to haematology and ICU
items: Suspected acute chest syndrome, SpO2 below 95% on air or falling, new neurological signs, priapism lasting more than 4 hours, Hb 2 g/dL or more below baseline, sepsis, or pain uncontrolled despite escalating opioids.
Pregnant patients with SCD: involve obstetrics early; manage as high-risk pregnancy.
Rising bilirubin with RUQ pain, sudden splenic enlargement with falling Hb, or reticulocytopenia: urgent haematology review for hepatic crisis, sequestration or aplastic crisis.

sections.title: Hydroxyurea and long-term care (NSCAEM)
items: Offer hydroxyurea to adults with repeated acute chest syndrome, more than 3 crises a year needing hospitalisation, or recurrent pain affecting daily life (NSCAEM operational guidelines).

Hydroxyurea: start 10 to 15 mg/kg/day orally once daily; escalate every 6 to 8 weeks if counts allow, up to a maximum of 35 mg/kg/day. Monitor CBC during titration. Lower doses in CKD. Clinical benefit takes 3 to 6 months.
Stop hydroxyurea 3 months before planned conception; counsel on contraception and adherence (do not double missed doses).
Folic acid 5 mg daily, vaccination as per national guidelines, hydration, avoiding temperature extremes, and an individual pain care plan.

The National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) provides screening, sickle cell status cards, free hydroxyurea, folic acid and transfusion through NHM facilities; offer genetic and premarital counselling.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Delaying analgesia or labelling patients as drug-seeking.
Aggressive IV fluid boluses causing pulmonary oedema.
Missing evolving acute chest syndrome on day 2 to 3 of admission, or missing malaria and sepsis as triggers.
Transfusing uncomplicated crises, or overtransfusing above Hb 10 g/dL.

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.dose: 0.1 mg/kg IV or SC, repeat every 30 to 60 minutes titrated to pain and sedation
drugs.notes: Use the individual care plan dose if available. Reduce in elderly and renal impairment. Monitor sedation and respiratory rate.

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 1 g orally or IV every 6 hours, maximum 4 g/day

drugs.name: Ibuprofen
drugs.dose: 400 mg orally three times daily for 5 to 7 days
drugs.notes: Avoid in renal impairment, peptic ulcer, anticoagulation or pregnancy.

drugs.name: Ketamine (subanaesthetic)
drugs.dose: 0.1 to 0.3 mg/kg/hour IV infusion, maximum 1 mg/kg/hour
drugs.notes: Refractory pain in hospitalised patients, monitored setting.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
drugs.dose: Ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV once daily plus azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily

drugs.name: Hydroxyurea
drugs.dose: Start 10 to 15 mg/kg/day orally once daily, increase every 6 to 8 weeks to a maximum of 35 mg/kg/day
drugs.notes: Monitor CBC; lower dose in CKD; stop 3 months before conception.
